title: No. 5 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning Dangers From Foreign Force and Influence) (Jay)
paragraphs: Queen Anne, in her letter of July 1, 1706, to the Scottish Parliament, makes some observations on the importance of the UNION then being formed between England and Scotland that deserve our attention. I will share with the public one or two extracts: "An entire and perfect union will be the solid foundation of lasting peace: It will secure your religion, liberty, and property; remove the animosities among yourselves, and the jealousies and differences between our two kingdoms. It must increase your strength, riches, and trade; and by this union the whole island, being joined in affection and free from all apprehensions of different interest, will be ENABLED TO RESIST ALL ITS ENEMIES." "We most earnestly recommend to you calmness and unanimity in this great and weighty affair, that the union may be brought to a happy conclusion, being the only EFFECTUAL way to secure our present and future happiness, and disappoint the designs of our and your enemies, who will doubtless, on this occasion, USE THEIR UTMOST ENDEAVORS TO PREVENT OR DELAY THIS UNION."

It was noted in the previous paper that weakness and divisions at home would invite dangers from abroad, and that nothing would do more to secure us from them than union, strength, and good government within ourselves. This subject is rich and cannot easily be exhausted.

The history of Great Britain is the one with which we are generally best acquainted, and it offers us many useful lessons. We may profit from their experience without paying the price it cost them. Although it seems obvious to common sense that the people of such an island should be only one nation, we find that they were for ages divided into three, and that those three were almost constantly embroiled in quarrels and wars with one another. Despite the fact that their true interests with respect to the continental nations were really the same, the arts, policies, and practices of those nations kept their mutual jealousies perpetually inflamed, and for a long series of years they were far more inconvenient and troublesome than they were useful or helpful to each other.

Should the people of America divide themselves into three or four nations, would not the same thing happen? Would not similar jealousies arise and be likewise nurtured? Instead of being "joined in affection" and free from all apprehension of different "interests," envy and jealousy would soon extinguish confidence and affection, and the partial interests of each confederacy, rather than the general interests of all America, would be the only objects of their policies and pursuits. Hence, like most other BORDERING nations, they would always be either embroiled in disputes and war, or living in constant fear of them.

The most enthusiastic advocates of three or four confederacies cannot reasonably suppose they would long remain on equal footing in strength, even if it were possible to form them so at first. But, granting that this were practicable, what human contrivance can secure the continuance of such equality? Apart from local circumstances that tend to generate and increase power in one part and to impede its progress in another, we must consider the effects of that superior policy and good management which would probably distinguish the government of one above the rest, and by which their relative equality in strength and standing would be destroyed. For it cannot be assumed that the same degree of sound policy, prudence, and foresight would uniformly be observed by each of these confederacies for a long succession of years.

Whenever, and from whatever causes, it might happen—and happen it would—that one of these nations or confederacies should rise on the scale of political importance well above her neighbors, that moment those neighbors would view her with envy and fear. Both passions would lead them to encourage, if not actively promote, whatever might reduce her importance, and would also restrain them from measures intended to advance or even to secure her prosperity. It would not take much time for her to discern these unfriendly attitudes. She would soon begin not only to lose confidence in her neighbors, but also to feel a disposition equally unfavorable toward them. Distrust naturally creates distrust, and nothing more quickly turns goodwill and kind conduct into hostility than invidious jealousies and unfair imputations, whether spoken or implied.

The North is generally the region of strength, and many local circumstances make it likely that the most Northern of the proposed confederacies would, at no distant time, be unquestionably more formidable than any of the others. No sooner would this become evident than the NORTHERN HIVE would arouse the same ideas and feelings in the more southern parts of America that it formerly did in the southern parts of Europe. Nor is it a rash conjecture that its young swarms might often be tempted to gather honey in the more blooming fields and milder air of their luxurious and more delicate neighbors.

Those who carefully study the history of similar divisions and confederacies will find ample reason to fear that the ones being contemplated would be neighbors only in the sense that they would border one another; that they would neither love nor trust each other, but on the contrary would be a prey to discord, jealousy, and mutual injuries. In short, they would place us exactly in the position in which some nations doubtless wish to see us—FORMIDABLE ONLY TO EACH OTHER.

When did the independent states into which Britain and Spain were formerly divided ever combine in such alliance, or unite their forces against a foreign enemy? The proposed confederacies will be DISTINCT NATIONS. Each would have to regulate its commerce with foreigners through separate treaties; and since their products and commodities are different and suited to different markets, those treaties would be essentially different. Different commercial concerns must create different interests, and so different degrees of political attachment to and connection with different foreign nations. Hence it might, and probably would, happen that the foreign nation with whom the SOUTHERN confederacy was at war would be the one with whom the NORTHERN confederacy most wished to preserve peace and friendship. An alliance so contrary to their immediate interest would not therefore be easy to form, nor, if formed, would it be observed and fulfilled with perfect good faith.

Indeed, it is far more probable that in America, as in Europe, neighboring nations, acting under the impulse of opposite interests and unfriendly passions, would frequently take different sides. Considering our distance from Europe, it would be more natural for these confederacies to fear danger from one another than from distant nations, and therefore that each of them would be more eager to guard against the others through foreign alliances than to guard against foreign dangers through alliances among themselves. And here let us not forget how much easier it is to receive foreign fleets into our ports and foreign armies into our country than it is to persuade or compel them to leave. How many conquests did the Romans and others make in the role of allies, and what changes did they introduce, under that same role, into the governments of those they pretended to protect.
Let candid men judge, then, whether dividing America into any given number of independent sovereignties would tend to secure us against the hostilities and improper interference of foreign nations.
